## My data

The Fairness dataset is the ACS Income NC dataset from Fairlearn. Each 
row represents one person, and the dataset contains 5,000 rows. The data is based on American Community Survey information.
The Sports dataset is the 10 MLB Pitchers 2015–2019 dataset. Each row represents 
one pitch, and the dataset contains 33,289 rows. It contains information about 
pitch types, pitch results, and release speeds.

```{r}
#| label: data
#| echo: true
```

## Part A · Fairness

**My group:** sex **My outcome:** income >= 50000

**Question A:** "Of each sex (group), what share has at least $50,000? (outcome)?"
**Question B:** "Of everyone with an income of at least $50,000 (outcome), what share is each
sex? (group)?"

### A0 · My group and my outcome

```{r}
#| label: a0
#| echo: true
```

```{r}
#| label: a0-check
#| include: false
```

### A1 · The rate within each group (question A)

```{r}
#| label: fig-a1
#| ref.label: a1
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Share of each group with the outcome."
#| fig-alt: "The plot compares the share of males and females who have an income of at least $50,000."
```

```{r}
#| label: a1-check
#| include: false
```

I predicted that males would have a higher rate of income above $50,000 than females. The plot allows me to compare the percentage of each group that reaches this income level. Each bar represents its own group's total, making it possible to compare groups fairly even when they have different numbers of people.

### A2 · Rates with their standard error

```{r}
#| label: fig-a2
#| ref.label: a2
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Rate in each group, with ± one standard error and the group size."
#| fig-alt: "The plot compares the income outcome rates for males and females with standard error ranges and group sizes."
```

```{r}
#| label: a2-check
#| include: false
```

The standard error ranges show how much uncertainty there is around each group's estimated rate. A smaller group will generally have a wider range because it has fewer observations. This helps readers recognize that smaller groups are still important and should not be ignored when comparing outcomes.

### A3 · Zoom or filter?

```{r}
#| label: fig-a3
#| ref.label: a3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Counts per group: from 0, zoomed and filtered."
#| fig-subcap: ["From 0", "Zoomed", "Filtered"]
#| fig-alt: "The three plots compare the number of people in each sex group using the original scale, a zoomed scale, and a filtered scale."
#| layout: [[1, 1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-check
#| include: false
```

The zoomed plot's Lie Factor (largest vs smallest group) is
`r round(a3_lie_factor, 1)`.

The original plot shows the full difference in group sizes starting from zero. The zoomed plot makes the difference easier to see but can make it appear larger than it really is. The filtered plot removes part of the scale and can be misleading because it hides some of the original data. I would publish the original plot because it shows the group sizes without exaggerating the difference.

### A4 · Each group's share of everyone with the outcome (question B)

```{r}
#| label: fig-a4
#| ref.label: a4
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Each group's share of everyone with the outcome."
#| fig-alt: "The plot shows how the people earning at least $50,000 are divided between males and females."
```

```{r}
#| label: a4-check
#| include: false
```

Question A compares the percentage within each sex, while question B compares how much each sex contributes to everyone who meets the income outcome. The results can point in the same direction, but they measure different things because the groups may have different sizes. Question A is the better choice when comparing income rates between groups.

## Part B · Sports

**My group, outcome and value:** My group is pitch_type, my outcome is result == "S", and my numerical value is release_speed.

### B0 · My group, outcome and value

```{r}
#| label: b0
#| echo: true
```

```{r}
#| label: b0-check
#| include: false
```

### B1 · The rate within each group

```{r}
#| label: fig-b1
#| ref.label: b1
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Share of each group with the outcome."
#| fig-alt: "The plot compares the percentage of pitches resulting in a strike across different pitch types."
```

```{r}
#| label: b1-check
#| include: false
```

The plot shows the percentage of pitches that resulted in strikes for each pitch type. Shares are more useful than raw counts because some pitch types may have been thrown much more often than others.

### B2 · A mean with its two spreads

```{r}
#| label: fig-b2
#| ref.label: b2
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Mean in each group, with ± one standard error and group size."
#| fig-alt: "The plot compares the average release speed for each pitch type with standard error ranges and sample sizes."
```

```{r}
#| label: b2-check
#| include: false
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-b2
#| tbl-cap: "Group size, mean, sd and se."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(b2_summary, digits = 3)
```

The plot compares average release speeds across pitch types. Standard deviation describes how spread out individual pitch speeds are, while standard error describes the uncertainty in each group's estimated mean. Comparing the means and these ranges helps show whether the differences between pitch types are meaningful.

### B3 · Zoom or filter?

```{r}
#| label: fig-b3
#| ref.label: b3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Counts per group: zoomed and filtered."
#| fig-subcap: ["Zoomed", "Filtered"]
#| fig-alt: "The two plots compare pitch counts using a zoomed scale and a filtered scale."
#| layout: [[1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: b3-check
#| include: false
```

The zoomed plot makes differences between pitch counts easier to see, while the filtered plot removes part of the data from view. A reader could think that the differences between pitch types are larger than they actually are. My sports dataset does not have a year, season, or date column available for this analysis, so I cannot compare changes over time.

### B4 · Each group's share of everyone with the outcome

```{r}
#| label: fig-b4
#| ref.label: b4
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Each group's share of everyone with the outcome."
#| fig-alt: "The plot shows each pitch type's share of all pitches that resulted in strikes."
```

```{r}
#| label: b4-check
#| include: false
```

B1 shows the percentage of pitches resulting in strikes within each pitch type. B4 shows how much each pitch type contributes to all pitches that resulted in strikes. The results can differ because pitch types are not thrown equally often.
